Follow the maths,
step by step.

Every result below updates with the simulator. Start with the formula and answer, then expand the substitutions, units and limitations.

Simple reference calculations +

These idealised vertical examples build intuition. They omit the ramp, attitude control and cooling, so they are not the full-stunt result.

01 JUST TO HOVER
Fhover = mg
19.6 kN

2,000 kg × 9.80665 m/s². Below this, an upright car cannot hover at its initial mass.

02 WITHOUT A LANDING BURN
v = √(2gh)
19.8 m/s

About 71 km/h straight down after 20 m, starting from rest. No drag or rotation.

03 IDEAL UPRIGHT LANDING
hburn = h · mg / F
6.54 m

Coast from rest, then burn at 60 kN: 0.80 s and 88 kg of gas at constant 550 m/s exhaust. Ignores the flip and cooling.

04 THE SUPPLY LIMIT
ṁ = F / ve
109 kg/s

At 60 kN and 550 m/s. The ideal full-tank hover-equivalent duration is 7.01 s; cooling, control, reserve and changing mass are omitted.

WHAT HOLDS IT UPSIDE DOWN?

A pressure difference,
spread over the floor.

S = Δp · A ≥ mg

Over an assumed sealed 4 m² floor, holding a 2,000 kg car stationary upside down needs at least 4.90 kPa of pressure difference: about 4.8% of atmospheric pressure.

Selected fan suction: 2.0× weight · static inverted hold passes.

At the top of a circular ramp, contact force is N = mv²/R + S − mg. The stationary condition above omits leakage, traction and structural margins.

SENSITIVITY / WHAT CHANGES THE ANSWER?

What changes
the result?

Run the current case plus twenty-six changed assumptions. The first rows compare feed diameter and the optimistic feed bound, because supply capacity decides the reviewed-baseline contact verdict. Most change one input; the regulator-and-throat case and final case combine inputs. Ramp energy and peak power reveal changes that leave the release state unchanged. These tests use the same physics as the replay and do not estimate a real-world success probability.

Run the audit for the current settings.

Contact speed includes rotation of the first touching point. Sideways speed, cold operating limit, gas supply and ramp checks can each reject a case. Material ratings, real internal fit, sensor faults and post-contact suspension dynamics remain unverified.

Reference nitrogen properties in flight

The default uses tables generated with CoolProp 8.0.0 and its reference nitrogen equation. Tank temperature, pressure and enthalpy are interpolated in entropy and log density; regulator temperature is interpolated in enthalpy and log pressure. The selected inputs set the initial entropy, so each run follows its own discharge path. Peng–Robinson remains an explicit comparison.

Interpolation is validated against independent off-grid reference states. Cells touching saturation or liquid states, and states outside the table domain, stop thrust and prevent a pass. Gas temperatures are predictions under the assumed tank and regulator processes, not measured component temperatures. Nozzle condensation, tank-wall heat transfer and actual materials still need separate models. Reference equation and provenance ↗

Detailed assumptions

Open only the group you want to change. Each input updates the replay and the calculations.

How fan leakage sets the power requirement +

Required pressure difference is Δp = S/A. Air enters through the skirt gap: effective leak area = perimeter × gap, plus a 4 cm² allowance. We calculate compressible orifice flow with discharge coefficient 0.65, then fan compression work divided by fan efficiency and 94% motor efficiency. The familiar approximation is Q ≈ Cᴅ L g √(2Δp/ρ), P ≈ Δp Q/η.

The selected electrical fan budget is an assumption. Achievable suction is limited by power, a 45 m/s fan-face flow screen and an approximate rotor-head limit. A real fan pressure/flow curve, duct losses, skirt dynamics and uneven surfaces remain unverified. Curvature also matters: for a flat sealed length ℓ on radius R, sagitta is R − √(R² − (ℓ/2)²). The screen requires 30 mm ride clearance plus this gap to fit within the selected seal travel. With the baseline 2.8 m sealed length and roughly 11 m surface radius this is about 120 mm, much larger than the residual 2 mm leakage gap. A separate quasi-static traction screen checks μ × driven-load-fraction × N against mg sin(pitch), with N = suction + mg cos(pitch) + mv²/R. The displayed static comparison assumes constant speed. Full-stunt mode additionally integrates the climb, fan buildup, speed control and shared battery demand. Fans generate adhesion only while sufficiently sealed against a surface.

Tank volume, mass and packaging assumptions +

The inventory occupies the selected internal water volume, split 2:1 between passenger-space and rear tanks. We add estimated vessel walls, 3 mm liner and 20 cm total end/fitting allowance to two hemispherical-ended cylinders. Changing the vessel performance index scales the assumed wall stress allowance with it; this is a sensitivity study, not a laminate design. The 400 L concept at baseline is roughly 1.72 m long × 0.70 m outside diameter.

Empty-vessel mass uses the selected pressure–volume/weight index (default 120 kJ/kg), consistent in scale with Hexagon Purus’s 700 bar, 360 L, 208 kg hydrogen cylinder. That catalogue cylinder is 2.06 m long and would exceed our 1.75 m passenger bay. Its dimensions and gas compatibility are not interchangeable with a custom nitrogen tank.

Battery, structure/drive unit/driver, fan modules, 70 kg of valves/plumbing/mounting allowance and stored gas all count toward minimum wet mass. The mass slider cannot physically undercut that budget: the model uses the larger value and flags the mismatch. All component allowances need design-specific validation.

Three different cooling mechanisms +

Tank blowdown lowers the temperature of the remaining gas. In real-nitrogen mode we follow a constant-entropy path interpolated from CoolProp reference nitrogen tables (or Peng–Robinson when explicitly selected). Pressure reduction through a regulator is a separate, approximately constant-enthalpy process: its Joule–Thomson temperature change is calculated from the same equation of state. An ideal gas has no Joule–Thomson temperature change.

Nozzle acceleration lowers static temperature again. A perfectly expanded ideal-gas calculation can enter nitrogen’s phase-change region; that prediction is a warning that a single-phase formula is inadequate, not a prediction of the actual jet temperature. The simulator uses an assumed effective exhaust velocity with a thermal energy cap, rather than resolving two-phase nozzle flow.

Cold affects exhaust performance, seals, valves, shrinkage and frost from moisture. Dry gas helps with water ice; it does not prevent gas cooling. Cells touching saturation or liquid states are conservatively flagged and stop thrust; single-phase gas below the critical temperature is allowed. States outside the reference table domain also stop thrust and fail the screen. Wall heat transfer, condensation, material qualifications and frosting rates are unresolved. Isothermal mode supplies idealized external heat and is an optimistic comparison.

Other constraints before calling this a real design +

Supply and control: actual valve flow coefficients, line lengths and losses, pressure waves, off-axis jets, minimum pulse width, sensors, latency and redundant control. The selected feed diameter is an aggregate equivalent flow area, possibly several parallel lines, not an assumed single hose.

Vehicle dynamics: measured inertia and centre of gravity, gas-distribution changes, full ramp traction, tyre forces, surface clearance, gyroscopic coupling, plume/ground interactions and suspension landing loads. The flight resolves six degrees of freedom with generic rectangular inertia and ten assumed nozzle positions; it is not a reconstruction of measured footage.

Power and structure: simultaneous battery discharge, fan/motor thermal limits, tank supports, crash isolation, pressure-vessel qualification, fatigue and a real occupancy/packaging model. The electric compressor does not supply the instantaneous jet power during flight; that energy was stored in the gas beforehand. Refill energy and time matter between attempts. This layout assumes offboard filling and includes no onboard compressor. For scale, an ideal-air reversible refill of 250 kg into 600 L at room temperature requires roughly 28 kWh; at 10 kW input and 50% overall efficiency, roughly 5.7 hours. Real nitrogen compression and cooling require a separate plant model.

MODEL / ASSUMPTIONS AND LIMITS

Inspectable assumptions.
Honest limits.

The full-stunt mode integrates a driven circular-ramp climb, then passes its actual position, velocity and rotation into the 3D gas-thruster model. Airborne-only mode remains available.

Model history · 4.3 +

What changed in 4.3

The default landing verdict changed from pass to fail: 0.990 → 1.659 m/s downward, above the selected 1.5 m/s limit. Version 4.2 used an optimistic feed bound that allowed nozzle pressure and gas flow that the assumed 85 mm feed could not deliver together. The new default solves their pressure/flow balance. The reference EOS is unchanged; the feed correction causes this verdict change.

With the other default inputs held fixed, 85 mm fails contact, 100 mm passes, and 120 mm does not bind the feed solve. These larger-feed cases still fail the cold-component screen. The independent bound remains a labelled comparison.

Motion, nozzles & control +

A 4.6 × 1.95 × 1.2 m rigid body uses quaternions, three-axis angular velocity, scaled rectangular inertia, fixed CG offsets and Euler’s rigid-body equations including gyroscopic terms. Seat specific acceleration also includes rotational terms; impact loads are not modeled. Four underside jets, four rear jets and two opposed nose-side jets apply individual positive-only forces and torques. Positions, ratings and flow geometry are assumptions.

The allocator solves a bounded force-and-moment tracking problem. Each jet has a choked-flow limit; all share finite feed capacity and gas inventory. A causal control-command delay and separate first-order valve response delay commanded thrust. A stuck-closed jet can be selected; ambient wind and attitude-dependent projected area affect drag. Roll, pitch, yaw and translation compete for that supply. Rotation direction, heading target and lateral target are explicit choices. The full-run preset continues inherited rotation and holds the release-track heading; the original controller remains a comparison preset. A stuck-closed jet has no dedicated recovery strategy. The generic controller is not Tesla’s.

Finite gas, cooling & pressure +

Default storage uses the reference nitrogen EOS through shipped CoolProp tables, initially at the selected ambient temperature (20°C by default). At 250 kg in 600 L and 20°C it gives approximately 492.5 bar; optional Peng–Robinson gives 440.6 bar and ideal air gives 351 bar. These are property-model outputs, not measured pressures. See the hardware section for tank mass, volume, geometry and thermal assumptions.

Cooling follows a constant-entropy remaining-gas path. The adjustable regulator defaults to 100 bar with 8% delivery loss; real-nitrogen outlet temperature follows constant enthalpy. A scalar pressure/flow solve couples the nozzle and aggregate feed geometry; effective exhaust speed falls with gas temperature. Expelled gas reduces vehicle mass. The thermal screen compares minimum flowing and tank temperatures with an explicitly assumed component operating limit. Isothermal operation additionally requires the calculated heat input; that heat is no longer free.

Reference table interpolation is checked against direct CoolProp states, with rejected phase and domain cells. The optional Peng–Robinson comparison remains an approximate model with known dense-gas bias. The default feed model solves a common nozzle-inlet pressure: feed inflow must cover clipped nozzle demand at that pressure, below the selected regulator/loss ceiling. The optional independent tank-to-ambient bound is optimistic and can pair unattainable pressure and flow. Both retain regulator temperature and exhaust speed at the pre-solve pressure ceiling; this hydraulic correction is not a full thermodynamic manifold or transient plenum model. No two-phase nozzle solution, detailed valve/pipe network, measured fan curve, compressor refilling, tank-wall heat transfer or structural qualification is resolved.

What counts as a landing? +

Simulation stops at the first contact of the rotating body envelope with level ground. A “soft touchdown” requires downward first-contact-point speed ≤ 1.5 m/s, sideways contact speed ≤ 1 m/s, forward/backward contact-speed magnitude ≤ 1.5 m/s, upright tilt ≤ 8°, and total angular speed ≤ 12°/s. These are chosen screening thresholds, not automotive safety standards.

CSV includes ramp/flight phase, first-point velocity, CG velocity, net thrust load, seat specific acceleration and feed diagnostics. Feed pressure, demand, capacity and residual refer to the integrated interval’s starting gas state, exported as feed_state_gas_kg; positive residual in the optimistic comparison exposes an unattainable pressure/flow pair. Experiment JSON includes landing checks and the latest sensitivity audit. A soft classification does not certify tire loads, suspension travel, occupant loads, structural integrity or runway clearance.

What the model cannot establish +

The model includes roll, pitch, yaw and ten-nozzle allocation. Ramp motion starts from rest at the foot of an assumed planar circular path, with drive, adhesion and power limits. A straight approach, curvature transition, wheel spin, axle load transfer and wind on the ramp are not resolved. Banked ramps are unsupported. Landing gear dynamics, detailed aerodynamics, uneven ramp contact and collisions after premature detachment are not simulated. The default carries the circular ramp’s angular rate into flight; extra release rates, wind, fixed CG offsets, inertia and a stuck-closed jet can be varied. Fan suction is power/flow limited on the surface and supplies no airborne lift.

A passing case meets only the modeled screening thresholds. It does not establish a buildable or safe design. A failed case establishes failure of this chosen controller and hardware combination; optimization or different geometry could change it. A packaging pass means only that idealized components fit assumed bays. Neither outcome verifies the original footage or Tesla’s undisclosed hardware.

SOURCES / WHAT IS KNOWN

Separate the spectacle
from the specifications.

The October 15, 2026 event in McGregor, Texas matches the ramp stunt. Tesla’s original clip describes suction on the ramp and cold-gas attitude control in flight. The specification gaps matter.

MANUFACTURER CLAIM01
250kg of gas

Reported full inventory across 600 L of pressure vessels, feeding 10 nozzles. This is stored compressed gas, not 600 L of ambient air.

Tesla event · 12:03–12:21 ↗
MANUFACTURER CLAIM02
80+kN rear thrust

The four rear-facing thrusters are quoted at over 80 kN combined. Their forward-driving force does not establish the underside landing thrust.

Tesla event · 17:54–18:07 ↗
PRIMARY SOURCE03
2distinct systems

A sealed fan system holds the car to the ramp. Once airborne, expelled gas supplies force and changes attitude. The fan suction does not follow it into the sky.

Tesla · The Ramp, description ↗
OPEN QUESTIONS04
?critical unknowns

Actual wet mass, three-axis inertia, nozzle flow curves, fan curves, internal packaging, gas state and synchronized flight telemetry.

Test assumptions in the simulator ↑
▶

Start with the original footage.

Compare the ramp clip with the full event. Manufacturer footage is a source to examine; our model is an independent calculation.

Watch Tesla’s ramp clip ↗

Three objections, tested.

“Air can’t lift a two-tonne car.”

It can if enough mass is expelled fast enough. The constraint is force and flow rate: F = ṁ vₑ, using an effective exhaust velocity.

“It would fall off while upside down.”

A sealed fan system can make suction greater than weight. McMurtry demonstrated this independently in 2025. Manufacturer’s demonstration ↗

“Then it can fly like an aircraft.”

The assumed full tank provides only seconds of hover-equivalent impulse. Climbing, rotating and braking all spend that supply. A successful hop does not establish sustained flight.

The useful skepticism concerns endurance and acceleration. In his own WIRED physics analysis ↗, Rhett Allain questions the short gas supply and occupant loads. His acceleration estimate concerns the separate jump over the vehicle lineup, rather than the ramp landing modeled here.
